articles.summary: The high-profile murder trial of Lindsay Clancy — which ended in a mistrial last week after a jury was unable to convict or acquit the Massachusetts mother in the 2023 strangling deaths of her three young children — put a renewed spotlight on postpartum psychosis, the severe psychiatric condition her lawyers say she was suffering from at the time. As attention moves on from the trial, some researchers want more concrete changes that could improve how postpartum psychosis is researched, treated and prevented. How that happens — and how quickly — is unclear. While some in the mental health community applaud the improvements in how postpartum psychosis is recognized, others think the condition needs a more formal diagnosis for better long-term research. But the overall medical consensus, researchers say, is that postpartum psychosis is treatable when diagnosed early, and that outcomes as severe as Clancy’s are incredibly rare. They hope the trial, which has spurred frank conversations online among mothers about the complexities of postpartum mood and anxiety disorders, can also lead to productive conversations between patients and doctors — instead of panic . articles.summary: My new essay in Civitas Outlook tries to trace modern-day constitutional law to that fateful day twenty-five years ago. Every generation has a defining moment. For my generation, it was September 11, 2001. But a quarter century later, more than 30 percent of Americans have no living memory of 9/11 . The conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq have wound down, Guantanamo Bay is mostly closed, and Ground Zero is a museum. articles.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. L ike most Americans, I spent September 11, 2001, filled with both rage and dread. articles.summary: The European Central Bank raised interest rates. Will the Fed follow? A quarter-point increase in baseline borrowing costs across the bloc came as officials warned of “upside” inflation risks and oil prices shot above $100 a barrel. Fed-funds traders are putting 64% odds that the Fed will do the same next week (arbitrage alert: the chances on Kalshi are a bit lower ). But the ECB’s only job is to manage inflation, while the Fed has a trickier dual task of managing both prices and employment, and so is keeping an eye on a labor market stuck in a “low hire, low fire” defensive equilibrium. Global central banks would prefer to move their interest rates together to avoid warping investment flows and currency markets. (Back in 1986, a Fed compromise was struck to let Germany and Japan cut first.) The post-Covid responses to inflation and, now, slower growth have upset that lockstep instinct as central banks tend to their own economies. — Liz Hoffman

articles.summary: What does Never Forget mean if I was not alive to see the Twin Towers fall? My father used to work in an office in downtown Manhattan, just a few blocks from the Twin Towers; only recently did I ask him to tell me about that day. He happened to be starting his commute to the office when the first plane hit the North Tower. Like everyone else, he assumed it was a freak accident — a small plane making a low pass before the airport. He decided to stop in the midtown offices instead, thinking the downtown subway would be a mess. By the time he got off in midtown, the second plane hit, and it was clear the nation was under attack. After the towers fell, he walked back to my family’s apartment, grabbed his camcorder, and filmed people sitting along Riverside, basking in the sunlight and looking on in horror as ambulance after ambulance rushed downtown, smoke rising against the blue sky. His office would later be the last building torn down in the wake of the attack; his only recovered items were a small ceramic heart with my sister’s footprints and a cookie jar she and my brother decorated for Father’s Day.
